sessions.description:
Data forensics is the statistical analysis of test data to detect unusual patterns that may be associated with test fraud. It is a valuable component of a testing organization’s security process that provides unique insight into exam response data.

This session first introduces data forensics, with emphasis on the types of results that can be obtained from data forensics and the statistics used to obtain those results. Representatives from the American Board of Surgery and the American Board of Internal Medicine will give examples of how their programs use the results of data forensics analysis. Discussion will include 1) how tests flagged with anomalous results are handled, 2) how data forensics results inform additional analyses and deeper investigations, and 3) how data forensics results are used to support program-level decisions and changes that improve test security and subsequently the validity of inferences made based on test scores.Learning Objectives: Understand what data forensics is and what kind of information it gives about exams, items, and test score validity.Understand the types of statistics used in data forensics analysis and what those statistics can detect.Understand how testing organizations can use data forensics to improve test security.

sessions.description:
Health professions are experiencing significant generational shifts as younger physicians enter training and practice with different expectations around communication, hierarchy, feedback, work–life integration, and professional identity. These shifts may influence how professionalism is understood, expressed, and assessed across the medical education continuum.

Certification organizations and specialty boards play an important role in defining and reinforcing professional standards that support patient trust, safe care, and effective team-based practice.

This interactive session will explore how generational differences may influence professional norms and expectations in health care and consider implications for certification programs. Through real-time audience polling, facilitated discussion, and scenario-based reflection, participants will examine examples of evolving communication styles, workplace expectations, and emerging questions related to digital professionalism and professional conduct.

Attendees will consider how certification organizations can uphold core standards of professionalism while remaining responsive to generational change. The session will conclude with practical considerations for boards seeking to support professionalism education, guidance, and assessment across the workforce.Learning Objectives: Describe generational trends influencing professional expectations among emerging professionals entering the workforce.Examine how generational shifts may affect professionalism standards and assessment in certification programs.Identify strategies certification organizations can use to reinforce professionalism across generations.

sessions.description:
In this session, representatives from three boards will highlight current assessment innovation initiatives designed to reshape and enhance their certification programs.

First, the concept and importance of innovation in the Member Board community will be introduced. This section will focus on a brief description of how the American Board of Pediatrics’ (ABPeds’) current strategic plan is designed to advance assessment innovation as an organizational priority and enhance their certification program, including a description of facilitators and barriers to this work.

Next, the American Board of Anesthesiology (ABA) will describe its development of Resident Reach, a new longitudinal, formative assessment platform designed distinctly for residents and their program faculty. The Resident Reach platform will provide ongoing, low‑stakes assessment and feedback on medical knowledge, with the goal of supporting learning and skill development across the training continuum. Resident Reach is intended to spark discussion and coaching, it is not a question bank or an exam, and was inspired by the ABA’s MOCA Minute model.

Finally, experience piloting a key features testing paradigm in Thoracic Surgery (ABTS), based in part on the Canadian licensing system, will be reviewed. Data will be shared on this experience and how the learning led to changes to content development for the Thoracic Surgery oral exam. In addition, they will discuss their experience integrating AI into item generation.

Collectively, these presentations and the planned interactive panel discussion represents an opportunity to discuss innovative assessment efforts across three boards with substantially different sizes and resources and provide a framework for other boards to consider as they evolve their certification programs.Learning Objectives: Upon completion of this session, participant will be able to...Describe the concept of innovation and the importance of innovation for training programs and ABMS member boards.Upon completion of this session, participant will be able to....Discuss the value of a trainee engagement strategy and value of a longitudinal assessment program for learners.Upon completion of this session, participant will be able to...Explain the challenges and benefits of using Artificial Intelligence to facilitate generation of items for certification assessments.

sessions.description:
As certification programs confront rapid advances in artificial intelligence, evolving expectations of accountability, and increasing pressure to demonstrate relevance, long-standing assumptions about assessment are being challenged. This 60-minute interactive session brings together four measurement experts, two from ABMS member boards and two external experts, for a structured, debate-style exploration of how certification and continuing certification will evolve.

The session will focus on three core debate topics: (1) whether “knowledge” assessment should change in the age of AI; (2) whether patient outcomes are defensible measures of individual physician competence; and (3) the appropriate level of content customization in high-stakes certification and longitudinal assessment programs.

For each topic, panelists will present contrasting viewpoints in a moderated debate format, followed by a brief “clock-off” dialogue to surface nuance, tradeoffs, and areas of convergence. Attendees will be invited to vote on positions and propose additional questions for discussion. The session is designed to provoke thoughtful discussion, challenge default assumptions, and equip leaders to make informed, strategic decisions about innovation in assessment design.Learning Objectives: Evaluate competing perspectives on how artificial intelligence should influence the definition and assessment of physician knowledge in initial and continuing certification.Assess the strengths and limitations of using patient outcomes (including case logs) as indicators of individual physician competence in initial and continuing certification contexts.Identify key tradeoffs associated with increased assessment content customization in certification programs and their implications for validity, fairness, and public trust.

sessions.description:
Professionalism lapses during training are associated with subsequent challenges including board certification. Although numerous remediation strategies have been described, most programs focus on a single group (e.g., students, residents, or faculty). This interactive panel will explore professionalism remediation in undergraduate medical education (UME), graduate medical education (GME), and among physicians in practice to identify shared principles, highlight meaningful differences, and elevate best practices across career stages.

Intro (10 min)
Speakers will review the negative impacts of unprofessional behavior on patient care and summarize evidence linking professionalism lapses in training to subsequent challenges with board certification and maintenance.

Interactive presentation (20 min)
Speakers with expertise in professionalism remediation at the UME, GME and faculty levels will each describe their program / approach, including assessing the context in which the lapse occurred, the competency framework used to set and measure professionalism expectations, and remediation strategies for each setting. Audience response questions will be used to prompt participant engagement.

Discussion (20 min)
In small groups, participants will discuss examples of professionalism lapses among students, residents and practicing physicians to identify similarities and differences in addressing the concern based on the individual’s role.

Report out and wrap up (10 min): Participants will share insights with the larger group, facilitating synthesis of best practices in professionalism remediation that are applicable across the continuum of training and practice. Speakers will close with take home points and Q&A.Learning Objectives: Describe the link between early professionalism lapses and later certification or practice challenges.Analyze how contextual assessment and competency frameworks guide remediation decisions for students, residents and practicing physiciansApply cross-continuum insights to strengthen professionalism oversight and remediation policy

sessions.description:
This session reviews two initiatives modernizing medical assessment through advanced psychometrics and AI.

The first introduces a framework for evaluating clinical reasoning under uncertainty using the Script Concordance Test (SCT). Unlike traditional formats relying on discrete correct answers, the SCT probes diagnostic reasoning in ambiguous, real-world scenarios — precisely where expert judgment matters most. A novel psychometric model scores physicians' ability to differentiate and weigh clinical data, moving beyond binary scoring to capture the full spectrum of expert reasoning. This reflects the recognition that clinical expertise is defined not by certainty, but by the capacity to navigate ambiguity with nuance. An AI-driven feedback layer complements this by replacing standardized critiques with personalized guidance — initiating reflective questions, addressing learner-specific responses, and targeting individualized growth areas.

The second initiative leverages AI to resolve systemic pain points in the assessment lifecycle. It focuses on establishing a structured roadmap for future AI initiatives and implementing low-resource projects for immediate application, shifting technical workflow burden away from our team to enable higher-level strategic focus. An AI multi-agent framework streamlines high-stakes exam production while enhancing quality control and scalability.

Together, these initiatives advance a cohesive agenda: reconceptualizing clinical competence in ambiguous diagnostic contexts, establishing a new paradigm for individualized feedback, and building operational infrastructure to drive productivity and scale rigorous medical certification.Learning Objectives: Review clinical decision-making under uncertainty by applying script concordance testing and a novel psychometric scoring modelDemonstrate personalized feedback leveraging a Large Language Model.Understand the steps to streamline operational processes of an assessment lifecycle.

sessions.description:
Medical certifying boards play a critical role in upholding standards of excellence, public trust, and professional accountability. Strengthening organizational culture, particularly around collaboration, transparency, and engagement, can enhance fairness and reinforce confidence in the certification process.

Historically, organizations have kick-started their culture change initiatives with trainings, diversity workshops, awareness programs, and celebratory events. These programmatic activities are important early steps in raising awareness and building momentum. However, research and practice-based experiences show that to achieve lasting culture change and measurable progress, these efforts must mature beyond isolated programs.

In other words, organizations need to shift from ad-hoc initiatives to systemic, long-term strategies that are embedded throughout the organization to build resilient and sustainable programs.

This session will highlight why moving beyond this stage is both challenging and crucial, as well as explore how to make that critical shift and why it’s essential for sustainable organizational outcomes. Drawing from organizational psychology and business management literature, we’ll examine how inclusive practices—when integrated into systems such as hiring, evaluation, and governance—can support long-term performance and resilience. By cultivating psychological safety and equitable opportunities for all employees, leaders can ensure longevity and development.

Participants will also discuss case studies of organizations that have matured their programs and have made progress in successfully demonstrating that true integration drives better results and lasting impact.Learning Objectives: Describe the evolution from programmatic to systemic equity and inclusion efforts, explaining why trainings and one-off programs alone often fall short, and how embedding these efforts into organizational systems leads to more sustainable culture change and business impact.Identify at least two organizational systems or processes that can be strengthened to foster transparency, engagement, and fairness—such as metrics development and data tracking, recruitment and hiring practices, or strategic planning.Apply frameworks and best practices for embedding inclusive values into organizational infrastructure, including leadership accountability, governance structures, and day-to-day operations, thereby ensuring that these initiatives center psychological safety and equitable opportunities for all employees and are aligned with and embedded into the overall business strategy.

sessions.description:
Implementation Science (IS) is the scientific study of methods and strategies that facilitate the uptake of evidence-based practice and research into regular use. IS methods and frameworks have been used extensively to identify influences on health professional behavior related to the implementation of evidence-based recommendations for patient care. IS seeks to systematically close the gap between what we know and what we do. In very non-scientific language, IS is a method of understanding how best to help people ‘Do the Thing’ we want them to do. As a field, IS has been underutilized as a tool for improving medical education. Applying IS frameworks and principles to surgical education has the potential to facilitate the successful enactment of new educational practices by examining individual and systems level factors that impact behavior.

Session Format: This session is designed to be an interactive experience. Attendees will be engaged in small group work with rotating facilitators. There will be 3 main themes within the workshop: (1) Introduction to Implementation Science theories and frameworks, (2) Examples of Implementation Science in medical education, and (3) Facilitated application of an Implementation Science framework to an institution-specific problem.

Participants will be provided with handouts to provide a framework for planning and discussion. Rotating subject matter experts (workshop speakers) will serve as facilitators during the process. sessions.description:
As part of the American Board of Physician Medicine and Rehabilitation (ABPMR) Continuing Certification program, diplomates must submit an IHHC project once every five years. This results in over 1500 project submissions each year.

Prior to 2026, every submission was reviewed manually by an ABPMR Board Member. The resulting workload was not sustainable, so several changes have been made in 2026 to improve this process.

One adjustment was to bring on additional volunteer reviewers. The other change, which is the focus of this presentation, was to launch a pilot program using an AI LLM to review every submission.

Diplomate submissions are made through an online platform. The resulting submission is fed to an AI LLM and an email with the AI's determination is sent to a staff member. This determination is included when the review task is assigned to a volunteer reviewer. The diplomate does not see the AI's feedback about their submission. The reviewer uses the AI feedback to help inform their manual review.

This presentation will cover the LLM system prompt strategy used, along with the project genesis, initial testing, pilot phase, and update of the current state of things. It will explore the different technologies involved and the ways the human reviewers use the AI feedback they are given. It will also include feedback from our volunteers using the system and explore the road ahead for this project.Learning Objectives: Upon completion, participant will be able to describe how ABPMR is using an AI LLM in a real-world setting to reduce volunteer workload.Upon completion, participant will be able to list the pros and cons of involving AI with submission review tasks.

2-Sigma Reasoning: AI-Powered Precision Education for Clinical Decision Making

2-Sigma Reasoning is an AI virtual patient platform developed at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine with support from the ABIM Foundation. Learners interview a simulated patient in natural conversation, take a history, examine, order tests, commit to a differential, and manage the case. The patient responds to their decisions, so learners can explore the different approaches to clinical reasoning or managing a patient, something a written case cannot offer. An AI supervisor provides individualized feedback on their reasoning after every encounter, with no faculty proctoring required, so learners get autonomy, repetition, and low-stakes deliberate practice on demand. Each encounter also generates detailed data on how clinicians reason, supporting a research program that maps reasoning pathways across the continuum from medical students to practicing diplomates. The platform reflects four years of development, testing, and refinement, with four research papers published or under review. Attendees can work through a live case and learn how their board communities can participate in the study.

Specialty boards have never had the luxury of standing still. On one side, science evolves, workforce pipelines shift, and the definition of competency keeps getting refined. sessions.description:
Competency-based medical education (CBME) was built to answer a single question: how do we grant progressive autonomy to a powerful, imperfect, developing entity in service of the patient? Traditionally, that entity was always a trainee. Now there is a new entity – artificial intelligence (AI). As providers and health systems increasingly accept, rely on, and cede autonomy to AI in clinical care, the infrastructure for deciding how much autonomy, under what conditions, and with what oversight has not kept pace. Through CBME, the field of medical education has spent decades building exactly this infrastructure for physician trainees. The same framework and its lessons apply directly to AI.

This session maps key principles of CBME onto AI in healthcare: (1) Outcomes defined by patient and societal needs as the starting point for what gets built, funded, and prioritized. (2) Competency frameworks that define what a trustworthy entity looks like before granting autonomy. (3) Entrustment decisions calibrated to demonstrated competence, context, and risk. (4) Programmatic assessment through structures that aggregate individual judgments into system-level decisions. (5) Governance architecture (training programs, accrediting bodies, certifying bodies) that ensures accountability to the public.Learning Objectives: Map key principles of CBME onto AI in healthcare, identifying how each addresses a gap in current approaches to clinical AI deployment.Apply the concept of entrustment-based decision-making to clinical AI scenarios, calibrating progressive autonomy to demonstrated competence, context, and risk.Propose governance structures for clinical AI modeled on existing CBME infrastructure, including competency committees and certification bodies.

sessions.description:
As AI-enabled systems increasingly influence documentation, decision support, and quality measurement, clinicians must possess informatics competencies to engage with these tools safely, transparently, and responsibly. However, informatics expectations for physicians remain poorly defined and inconsistently embedded within existing competency frameworks, milestones, and certification standards. Compounding this challenge is a parallel lack of informatics expertise in the workforce; of the over one million board certified physicians in the US, only 3000 (0.3%) are board certified informaticians.

CBME provides a natural structure for addressing this gap, yet few specialties have made informatics competence explicit within CBME implementation. Surgical training represents an early and mature model of CBME adoption, with widespread use of EPAs and digitally mediated assessment workflows. Leveraging this environment, our group has deployed educational content, examined how informatics-related skills are implicitly required, variably demonstrated, and inconsistently assessed across established surgical training and educational pathways.

During this work, we have identified recurring informatics domains essential for effective participation in CBME and contemporary clinical practice, including data interpretation, digital workflow navigation, assessment documentation quality, and longitudinal performance analysis. Building on surgery as an initial model, we present a scalable, specialty-agnostic approach to embed informatics competence into CBME and certification frameworks, supporting a physician workforce prepared to practice in an AI-enabled healthcare environment.Learning Objectives: Identify the core informatics and artificial intelligence competencies required for contemporary clinical practice using a competency-based medical education framework.Describe actionable assessment strategies capable of evaluating clinical informatics and artificial intelligence competence using workplace-based and EPA-aligned evidence.Evaluate pathways for integrating Clinical Informatics training into existing training programs that prepare the clinician for artificial intelligence-enabled health systems.

sessions.description:
The United States does not produce enough physicians domestically to fill its residency programs. The gap between U.S. medical school graduates and available residency positions has been filled for many years by international medical graduates (IMGs), both U.S. citizens who were educated abroad and foreign nationals. Comprising roughly 25% of active physicians, IMGs are not a supplement to the domestic supply; they are a structural necessity, and disproportionately so in primary care and in rural, urban, and underserved communities.

Understanding what threatens this pipeline is urgent. This presentation opens with a data-driven profile of IMG contributions, with focus on medically underserved areas where unmet need is most acute. From that foundation, presenters examine contemporary developments with real potential to impact the IMG pipeline, both positively and negatively: significant changes in U.S. immigration policy and visa processing; the growing number of states creating alternative licensing pathways for internationally trained physicians; and the continuing shortfall in domestic medical school capacity relative to available residency positions. Together these forces shape how many physicians are available to train in and serve U.S. communities.

The presentation draws on data and insights from Intealth’s decades of experience through ECFMG Certification, primary-source credential verification, J-1 visa sponsorship, and research on IMG distribution in U.S. health care.Learning Objectives: Upon completion, participants will be able to describe the structural gap between U.S. physician production and residency demand, and the role IMGs play in filling that gap.Upon completion, participants will be able to identify key developments that affect the IMG pipeline and the availability of physicians to train in and serve U.S. communities.Upon completion, participants will be able to access data on IMG contributions and apply these data to articulate the consequences of pipeline disruptions for access to care.

sessions.description:
The physician workforce in the United States (US) is struggling to keep pace with rapidly growing healthcare demands. Aging populations and expanding healthcare needs are major factors contributing to the physician shortage. As demand rises, internationally trained medical graduates (IMGs) represent an important and often underutilized resource.

IMGs make up roughly one quarter of the active physician workforce and are more likely than US-trained physicians to practice in medically underserved areas. Despite their contributions, IMGs often face significant barriers, including complex licensing requirements, residency placement challenges, visa restrictions, and differences in medical education systems. Many highly qualified physicians must repeat training or spend years navigating certification processes before they can practice in the US.

Illinois is among the first states to introduce policies focused on alternative pathways to integrate IMGs into the US healthcare workforce. These pathways maintain consistent standards of medical knowledge, clinical competence, and patient safety while allowing qualified IMGs to enter practice more efficiently.

Traditional licensing typically requires IMGs to repeat residency training even if they have already practiced for years in their home countries. Alternative licensing pathways aim to better utilize this global talent while maintaining high standards of care.

sessions.description:
The rapid expansion of digitally driven care—telehealth visits, algorithmic decision support, patient portals, wearable data streams—has reshaped how patients encounter the healthcare system, often without reshaping the relational foundations that sustain trust. At the same time, health information now circulates widely across digital platforms, exposing patients to a mix of credible guidance, opinion, and misinformation. This is a symptom of eroding institutional trust.

When confidence in institutions and expertise weakens, conflicting narratives gain traction and the shared understanding that underpins the patient–physician relationship can fray. Without intentional transparency, digital literacy, and reaffirmation of professional accountability, technology and misinformation together threaten to erode the relational trust that has long been central to high-quality care.

Paradoxically, a recent survey indicated that board certification was important to 93% of respondents and was also one of the top factors contributing to choice of physician. The respondents also believed that board certified physicians provide higher quality care than physicians who are not certified.

Board certification can promote trust in the patient-clinician relationship by ensuring clinical judgment remains primary, even when technology is involved. In an era when patients encounter conflicting health information and digitally delivered care, certification serves as validation that a physician has met rigorous training requirements and continues to demonstrate clinical knowledge and expertise. Board certification has the ability to restore trust and professionalism in a digital, information-rich care environment.Learning Objectives: Upon completion, participants will be able to examine how digitally mediated care and technology integration are reshaping the moral and relational foundations of the patient–physician relationship.Upon completion, participants will be able to explain how health misinformation undermines professional authority, shared decision-making, and trust in clinical encounters.Upon completion, participants will be able to describe how board certification is valued by patients and can serve as a foundation for promoting trust and professionalism in a digital and information-rich healthcare environment.

In this model, physicians respond to questions tied to specific journal articles or synopses of new/evolving literature, demonstrating comprehension, critical analysis, and the ability to apply new knowledge to clinical practice.

Three American Board of Medical Specialties Member Boards—American Board of Emergency Medicine (ABEM), American Board of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ABOG), and American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN)—have incorporated article-based assessment into their continuing certification programs. Although they share a common goal, each board has developed a distinct implementation strategy.

In this session, representatives from these boards will discuss their program designs, guiding principles, and operational frameworks, including article/content curation, question development, psychometric considerations, and approaches to balancing standardization with personalization. They will also review analyses of user feedback, perceived relevance, and overall experience.

ABEM will describe its approach to translating rapidly evolving medical advances into accessible assessment content; ABOG will present findings from a research study examining the accuracy of large language models in answering article-based questions; and ABPN will share analyses of item performance by article and question type, physician subgroup performance, and survey results related to utility and satisfaction. Panelists will conclude by sharing lessons learned from pilot testing and operational rollout, highlighting successes and opportunities for improvement.Learning Objectives: describe the purposes and core features of article-based assessment as a component for continuing certification programscompare and contrast how different ABMS Member Boards design and implement their article-based assessmentidentify key lessons and insights learned from implementing article-based assessment

sessions.description:
Measuring physician competency beyond medical knowledge remains one of certification's most persistent challenges. Interpersonal communication skills are critical to patient outcomes yet notoriously difficult to assess at scale. This session presents a two-stage research program addressing that gap.

First, we describe the development of a unified physician competency model linking ACGME/ABMS competency domains to specialty-specific Milestones and the discrete, observable behaviors underlying each. This framework transforms abstract competency language into measurable behavioral indicators.

Second, we demonstrate how we trained a large language model (LLM) using the Calgary-Cambridge communication framework to analyze physician-patient transcripts — detecting whether specific interpersonal behaviors were present in real clinical encounters. This represents the first step toward scalable, automated communication assessment: moving from binary behavior detection toward quality rating at the behavior level.

Attendees will leave with a replicable framework for operationalizing competencies into measurable behaviors, and an understanding of how AI can serve as a scalable rater of communication skills — reducing dependence on direct observation and human rating burden.Learning Objectives: Translate specialty-specific Milestones into discrete, observable behaviors that can be operationalized for large-scale assessment across certification programs.Explain how LLMs can be trained to detect the presence of specific interpersonal communication behaviors in physician-patient transcripts using an established framework.Identify opportunities to apply AI-driven communication assessment within their certification programs as a scalable alternative to direct observation and human rating.

sessions.description:
Certification exams generate rich data about what physicians know — and where their knowledge gaps lie. Yet most diplomates receive only a score report or progress report. That report tells them how they did. It does not tell them what to do next.

ABIM's work on individualized learning uncovered two interconnected gaps. First, diplomates could benefit from richer, more actionable performance insights — not just item-level results, but patterns across time and topic areas that point toward specific learning needs. Second, even when a diplomate identifies a gap, they face a plethora of society resources with no clear map from "what I need to learn" to "where I should go."

This session presents a two-part solution developed in partnership with medical specialty societies. The first is an AI-driven feedback system that surfaces learning trends beyond scores — identifying patterns that diplomates and their advisors can act on. The second is a shared taxonomy: a common language co-developed between ABIM and societies that links what certification measures to what societies teach.

Together, these tools create a connected pathway: from assessment data, to personalized insight, to targeted learning resources. Attendees will see how this model works in practice and leave with a framework for building similar data partnerships between certification programs and the societies that serve their diplomates.Learning Objectives: Identify performance insight beyond item-level scores that certification data can provide to help diplomates better understand their learning needs.Describe how a shared taxonomy of topic areas, co-developed between a testing organization and medical specialty societies, improves the learner journey.Apply a framework for building or improving collaborative data partnerships between certification programs and specialty societies.

sessions.description:
Physicians, residents, and health care leaders face increasing demands on their time, making traditional communication methods less effective. Certification organizations must adapt how they share information to reach busy professionals through formats that fit into their daily routines.

This interactive panel will explore how the American Board of Emergency Medicine and the American Board of Orthopaedic Surgery have integrated podcasting into their communication strategies. Panelists will discuss how podcasts can translate complex information into concise, accessible audio content that listeners can engage with during commutes or other routine activities.

The session will also examine emerging technologies, including the use of AI tools to support podcast production. Panelists will discuss the benefits, limitations, and ethical considerations when using AI to support communication in the medical and certification environments.

Participants will be invited to share their own experiences with podcasts, audiocasts, and other digital communication channels. Through discussion and audience interaction, the session will explore how certification organizations can effectively deliver timely, credible information in an evolving digital media landscape.Learning Objectives: Identify strategies certification organizations can use to communicate with physicians through podcasting and other digital media.Understand tools you can use to support podcast production and communication workflows, including equipment, software, and AI.Evaluate opportunities and risks when using AI and audio platforms to share certification and medical information.

sessions.description:
Artificial intelligence tools are increasingly used to search, summarize, and synthesize medical literature, but their outputs can introduce both subtle and substantial risks.

This session uses a series of case studies to explore common pitfalls encountered when AI is used in the reading and writing of literature reviews for medical education and for certification. The presentation will focus on examining how AI can support targeted literature reviews, rather than its use in automating or conducting systematic reviews.

Each case study presents both a cautionary scenario, such as fabricated citations, oversimplified evidence synthesis, or invisible bias, followed by practical beneficial suggestions for responsibly harnessing AI in those situations.

Participants will leave with concrete techniques for evaluating AI generated content, strengthening transparency, and integrating AI into literature review workflows without compromising rigor, trust, or educational integrity.

AI does not replace the usual literature review process, but it reshapes where human judgment matters most. When used thoughtfully, AI can expose literature gaps, accelerate screening, and support transparency. When used carelessly, it can quietly erode rigor.Learning Objectives: Identify common risks associated with the use of AI in literature review work, including fabricated citations, oversimplified evidence synthesis, and invisible bias.Evaluate AI-generated literature summaries and citations by assessing accuracy, source traceability, and completeness in relation to the underlying evidence.

Dr. Newton has served as President and Chief Executive Officer of the American Board of Family Medicine (ABFM) since 2019. As an educator, Dr. Newton served as residency director in Family Medicine at UNC and co-led the I3 collaborative of 24 primary care residencies focused on clinical transformation in residency practices. He served as Vice Dean of Medical Education at UNC during which he led a Liaison Committee on Medical Education (LCME) review, expanded the school, established satellite campuses, developed new curricula in professionalism and population health and expanded significantly the enrollment of underrepresented minorities. Over the last 3 years, the ABFM has led a national effort to redesign family medicine residency education as a part of a “major revision” of Family Medicine residency standards.

As Director of North Carolina AHEC he led a large statewide health professions educational network working with five medical schools, all nursing schools and many other health profession education programs. North Carolina AHEC’s major focus is health workforce education for rural and underserved communities. Under his leadership, AHEC won major grants to spread innovation in primary care, developed a statewide digital continuing education platform, increased community-based residency programs, helped develop statewide programs for community health workers and started novel statewide educational programs to provide health careers exposure for undergraduates, introduce continuing interprofessional education, and address opiates, burnout and social drivers of health.

Dr. Newton’s scholarship has focused on the organization and effectiveness of health care. He has authored more than 175 peer reviewed publications, with over 80 published with students and residents. He has been PI on grants totaling more than $50,000,000, and served on the Board of Trustees of the North Carolina State Health Plan, responsible for health care for approximately 700,000 state and county employees and retirees. In 2016, he served as Senior Policy Advisor to the North Carolina Secretary of Health and Human Services, helping to prepare the Medicaid 1115 innovation waiver, plan rural residency expansion and develop quality metrics for Medicaid.

He has served nationally as President of the Association of Departments of Family Medicine and was the Founding Chair of the Council of Academic Family Medicine. He served on the Liaison Committee on Medical Education and is on the planning committee of the National Academy of Medicine’s Global Forum on Innovation in Health Professional Education. Dr. Newton was the founding Chair of the American Board of Medical Specialties Committee on Continuing Certification and serves on its Board of Directors.

Dr. Newton graduated from Yale University with a double major in biology and history, earning his medical degree from Northwestern University Medical School. After his residency and Chief Residency in Family Medicine at UNC, he completed the Robert Wood Johnson Clinical Scholars Program and a received a Master in Public Health from the UNC Gillings School of Global Public Health. He was selected as a Society of Teachers of Family Medicine Bishop Fellow, during which he also completed the American Council of Education Fellow’s program.

Dr. Newton is board certified by ABFM.

In these roles, she has worked to influence the direction of academic medicine and the continuum of medical education in ways aligned with UCSF’s approach to education, culture, and community.

Dr. Lucey joined UCSF in 2011 from The Ohio State University, where she was Vice Dean for Education for the College of Medicine and Associate Vice President for Health Sciences Education for the Office of Health Sciences. Ms. Bakare is the Co-Founder of Sickle Cell Prodigy, a patient-driven nonprofit redefining survivorship for individuals living with sickle cell disease who are exploring curative-intent therapies, including bone marrow transplant and gene-based therapy. A pioneering advocate in the rare disease community, she is recognized for advancing inclusion, challenging stigma, and elevating the patient voice at the intersection of medicine, media, and community.

Drawing from her lived experience, Ms. Bakare uses strategic storytelling and media engagement to shift perceptions and improve access to culturally responsive care. She serves in advisory roles across leading healthcare and biotech organizations, including the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, the American Board of Medical Specialties, Beam Therapeutics, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, Fulcrum, and Elevate Impact. She holds board positions with the Sickle Cell Knowledge & Information Network, Sickle Cell Disease Coalition, Sickle Cell Disease Partnership, and The Gift of Adoption Fund.

Diagnosed with the severe HbSS form of sickle cell disease in infancy, she underwent a successful allogeneic stem cell transplant in 2019 through a groundbreaking National Institutes of Health clinical trial. She is also the Founder of WBPR Agency, where she provides strategic communications counsel across healthcare, advocacy, and corporate sectors.

speakers.name: Brant J. Oliver, PhD, MS, MPH, FNP-BC, PMHNP-BC, LSSBB, CPXP
speakers.title: System Vice President for Care Experience, the Value Institute, Dartmouth Health Associate Professor, Departments of Community & Family Medicine, Psychiatry, and the Dartmouth Institute, Geisel School of Medicine  Director, Chronic Health Improvement Research Program at Dartmouth Health (CHIRP), Department of Community & Family Medicine  Executive Director, the Promise Partnership Coproduction Learning Health System, Dartmouth Health & Geisel School of Medicine
speakers.bio:
Dr. Oliver is Associate Professor at the Geisel School of Medicine and System Vice President for Quality and Safety for the Dartmouth Health System in New Hampshire. He has expertise in Learning Health Systems, coproduction and improvement measurement and methodology, and has served as principal investigator, co-investigator, improvement faculty, or methodologist for improvement, implementation and research collaboratives internationally in the U.S., Canada, U.K., Sweden, and Australia.

Dr. Oliver is the Executive Director of the Promise Partnership, a strategic collaboration between Dartmouth Health and Geisel which includes the Care Experience Collaborative, a multicenter initiative to improve human experience across the Dartmouth Health system.

He teaches graduate and doctoral students, residents, and post-doctoral fellows in improvement and implementation, specializing in measurement and analytics.

He is a board certified family and psychiatric nurse practitioner with over 20 years in practice, a majority of which is in multiple sclerosis neurobehavioral care. Dr. Oliver is the 2022 recipient of the national improvement and implementation science research award from the Quality and Safety Education for Nurses Institute, the 2023 recipient of the Batalden Award for career achievement in improvement from the Department of Veterans Affairs, and lead editor of the national best-selling Joint Commission Resources textbook Practical Measurement for Healthcare Improvement.

speakers.name: Laura L. Sessums, JD, MD, FACP
speakers.title: Chief Medical Officer, American Board of Internal Medicine
speakers.bio:
Laura Sessums joined the American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) as the Chief Medical Officer (CMO) in June 2025 and is a practicing general internist. Previously, she was the CMO at the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality where she had a diverse portfolio including Long COVID, strengthening collaboration with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) and other agencies, developing a primary care strategy, and improving patient experience measurement.

She has worked in the private sector, as the Chief Care Transformation Medical Director at Anthem, where she focused on commercial value-based care programs, including primary care,  Accountable Care Organizations, and episode-based payment models.

She also spent five years as the Director of the Division of Advanced Primary Care at the CMS Innovation Center (CMMI). At CMMI, she developed and launched the Comprehensive Primary Care Plus, America’s largest multi-payer initiative to improve primary care.

She spent more than a decade in academic medicine as a clinician-educator, mostly at Walter Reed Army Medical Center (as a civilian), where she served as the Chief of the General Medicine Section. Her professional activities have been in the areas of medical education and health care policy and advocacy; her research has focused on primary care.

Dr. Sessums is a former lawyer and is board certified by ABIM.

speakers.name: Richard E. Hawkins
speakers.title: President and Chief Executive Officer, American Board of Medical Specialties (ABMS)
speakers.bio:
Dr. Hawkins has more than 30 years of professional experience ranging from his service in the United States Navy as an officer in the Medical Corps to leadership positions at national medical professional associations.

Prior to joining ABMS in 2018, he served for five years as the Vice President for Medical Education Outcomes at the American Medical Association (AMA). There, Dr. Hawkins provided leadership for the AMA’s Accelerating Change in Medical Education initiative, a $13.5 million grant program supporting 32 medical schools that are transforming their educational programs to better prepare their students to succeed in the nation’s evolving health care systems. He also provided senior staff leadership to the AMA’s Council on Medical Education and Academic Physician Section.

Previously, Dr. Hawkins was the Senior Vice President for Professional and Scientific Affairs at ABMS. In this role, he led educational, assessment, and international initiatives. Prior to that, Dr. Hawkins was the Deputy Vice President and then Vice President for Assessment Programs at the National Board of Medical Examiners (NBME). There, he helped implement the Clinical Skills Examination of the United States Medical Licensing Examination, develop its assessment of professional behaviors program, and enhance the post-licensure assessment system for NBME and the Federation of State Medical Boards. Prior to joining NBME, Dr. Hawkins was Assistant Dean and Director of the Simulation Center at the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences. Additionally, he served in various academic appointments in the Naval Medical Corps, receiving numerous commendations for his service.

A well-respected leader in the fields of physician assessment and education, Dr. Hawkins has more than 20 years of experience working on various initiatives to evaluate and improve physician performance, and is co-editor of a textbook on the assessment of clinical competence. He has given more than 80 presentations; conducted 30-plus courses and workshops; and published more than 70 articles, books, and book chapters. Dr. Hawkins is Board Certified in Internal Medicine and Infectious Diseases by the American Board of Internal Medicine and is participating in continuing certification.
